questions.title: Ion with the highest concentration in basal saliva
questions.question: Which ion has the highest concentration in saliva under basal conditions?

explanations.A: Correct. Although potassium in saliva is about seven times its plasma level and bicarbonate about three times, the actual concentrations differ: basal salivary bicarbonate is roughly 50 to 70 mEq/L while potassium is about 30 mEq/L. Bicarbonate therefore has the highest absolute concentration in basal saliva. This is distinct from which ion is most concentrated relative to plasma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chloride is low in saliva, only about 10-15 percent of its plasma concentration, because it follows sodium reabsorption in the ducts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Potassium is high relative to plasma but its absolute concentration (about 30 mEq/L) is below that of bicarbonate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sodium is actively reabsorbed along the ducts, so its absolute concentration in saliva is low.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (Guyton ANSWERS section, item 5, correct = A) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that basal saliva has bicarbonate as its highest-concentration ion and low sodium and chloride.

questions.title: Ion most concentrated in saliva relative to plasma
questions.question: Compared with plasma, saliva has the highest relative concentration of which ion under basal conditions?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bicarbonate is enriched in saliva about threefold over plasma, less than potassium's roughly sevenfold enrichment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chloride is low relative to plasma (about 10-15 percent), following sodium reabsorption.
explanations.C: Correct. Salivary acini secrete a plasma-like fluid, but as it flows along the ducts sodium is actively reabsorbed and potassium is actively secreted in exchange. Potassium ends up about seven times its plasma concentration, the highest relative enrichment of any salivary ion. Bicarbonate is enriched about threefold, while sodium and chloride fall well below plasma levels.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sodium is reabsorbed in the ducts, leaving it well below its plasma concentration.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (Guyton ANSWERS section, item 12, correct = C) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that potassium is the salivary ion most concentrated relative to plasma, reflecting ductal reabsorption of sodium and secretion of potassium.

questions.title: Digestion most impaired in achlorhydria
questions.question: Digestion of which of the following is impaired to the greatest extent in patients with achlorhydria?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Carbohydrate digestion by salivary and pancreatic amylase and brush-border enzymes does not depend on gastric acid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fat digestion relies on bile salts and pancreatic lipase in the small intestine, not on gastric acid.
explanations.C: Correct. Achlorhydria means the stomach fails to secrete hydrochloric acid. Without acid, pepsinogen is not converted to pepsin, and any pepsin that forms cannot work because it needs an acid medium. Protein digestion, which begins in the stomach with pepsin, is therefore the most impaired.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nucleic acid digestion depends on pancreatic nucleases, not on gastric acid.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (Guyton ANSWERS section, item 8, correct = C) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: Explain that gastric acid is needed to form and activate pepsin, so achlorhydria most impairs protein digestion.

questions.title: Source of pepsinogen secretion
questions.question: The proenzyme pepsinogen is secreted mainly from which of the following structures?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pancreatic acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes such as trypsinogen and lipase, not pepsinogen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pancreatic ductal cells secrete a bicarbonate-rich fluid, not pepsinogen.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Duodenal epithelium secretes mucus and enteropeptidase, not pepsinogen.
explanations.D: Correct. Pepsinogen is secreted by the peptic (chief) cells of the gastric (oxyntic) glands. Contact with hydrochloric acid, or with pepsin itself, converts pepsinogen to active pepsin, which digests protein. It is therefore a product of the stomach's gastric glands.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (Guyton ANSWERS section, item 10, correct = D) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that pepsinogen is secreted by gastric chief (peptic) cells and activated to pepsin by acid.

questions.title: Hormone that decreases gastric emptying
questions.question: Which hormone is released by the presence of fat and protein in the small intestine and has a major effect in decreasing gastric emptying?

explanations.A: Correct. Cholecystokinin, released by fat and protein in the small intestine, is the only gastrointestinal hormone that inhibits gastric emptying under physiological conditions. It relaxes the orad stomach, raising its compliance so the stomach holds food longer, which is why fatty, protein-rich meals feel more filling. CCK also acts on brain feeding centres to reduce further eating.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide is an incretin stimulating insulin; it is not the physiological brake on gastric emptying named here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gastrin stimulates acid secretion and mucosal growth and does not physiologically slow emptying.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Motilin drives the interdigestive migrating motor complex rather than slowing emptying of a meal.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Secretin can slow emptying only at pharmacological doses; it is not the major physiological inhibitor.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (Guyton ANSWERS section, item 11, correct = A) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that CCK, released by fat and protein, is the only hormone that physiologically inhibits gastric emptying by relaxing the orad stomach.

questions.title: Structure that screens bolus size in swallowing
questions.question: Swallowing involves signalling between the pharynx and the brain-stem swallowing centre. Which structure is critical for determining whether a bolus of food is small enough to be swallowed?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The epiglottis swings back to cover the laryngeal opening and protect the airway; it does not screen bolus size.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The larynx is pulled upward and its cords approximate to guard the airway, not to gauge bolus size.
explanations.C: Correct. During the pharyngeal phase the palatopharyngeal folds on each side are pulled medially, forming a sagittal slit. This slit acts as a selective gate, letting adequately chewed food pass while impeding larger objects. It therefore determines whether a bolus is small enough to be swallowed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The soft palate is pulled upward to close the posterior nares and prevent nasal regurgitation, not to select bolus size.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The upper oesophageal sphincter relaxes to admit the bolus into the oesophagus but does not screen its size.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (Guyton ANSWERS section, item 25, correct = C) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that the palatopharyngeal folds form a slit that selects adequately chewed boluses during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing.

questions.title: Ion transport defect in cystic fibrosis
questions.question: In cystic fibrosis, mucus in exocrine glands becomes thick and blocks the ducts. A primary disruption in the transfer of which ion across cell membranes leads to the decreased secretion of fluid?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Calcium transport is not the primary defect in cystic fibrosis.
explanations.B: Correct. Cystic fibrosis is caused by defective chloride transport across the apical membrane of exocrine epithelial cells. The CFTR protein is a cAMP-regulated chloride channel; moving chloride out of the cell drives fluid secretion. When CFTR is absent or nonfunctional, chloride and therefore water secretion fall, so exocrine mucus becomes thick and blocks the ducts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phosphate handling is not the defective transport in cystic fibrosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Potassium transport is not the primary abnormality.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Although sodium and water movement are affected secondarily, the primary defect is in chloride (CFTR) transport.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (Guyton ANSWERS section, item 48, correct = B) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that cystic fibrosis is a defect of CFTR chloride transport, reducing exocrine fluid secretion and thickening mucus.
